title: Symbol Lock Timed Maze
description: This game is a grid-based puzzle where you move a player through a dark maze while managing a limited lantern charge. Your character has a configurable identity made of three attributes: shape, color, and rotation. Around the level there are special tiles that change one of those attributes when you step on them, so the core challenge is to route yourself through the maze in the right order to transform into the required configuration.Each level contains one or more requirement pads. Every pad expects a specific combination of shape, color, and rotation, shown through preview sprites in the level. When your current configuration matches one of those requirements, the game shows that you are “ready,” and if you step onto the corresponding pad it gets cleared. To finish the level, you have to clear all of the requirement pads. Movement also consumes lantern charge, unless you pick up a refill token that restores it. If you step onto a requirement pad with the wrong configuration, the game flashes an error instead of letting you solve it. If your lantern charge runs out, you lose a life and the level resets: your position, collected refills, solved pads, and current transformation state all go back to the start. After losing all lives, you lose the game.So overall, it is a timed transformation-and-routing puzzle: you explore a maze, modify your form, match the right symbolic state for each goal, manage limited energy, and try to solve all targets before your resets and lives run out.

title: Patter matching
description: The core of the game is a local 3×3 target kernel. Each puzzle contains one or more non-clickable goal kernels. A goal kernel is a large readable 3×3 device placed at the center of a local neighborhood. Its center square shows the target color. Its 8 surrounding preview squares indicate, in the exact same spatial arrangement as the live board around it, whether each surrounding live tile should end up the same color as the center or the opposite color. Use a very direct visual encoding: one preview color means “same as center,” the other means “opposite of center.” The player should be able to compare the preview and the surrounding live tiles position by position at a glance. Around each goal kernel are 8 large clickable live tiles, one in each neighboring position of the 3×3 neighborhood. These live tiles use only two colors, and the main interaction is that clicking a tile flips it from one color to the other. In the first level, clicking changes only that one tile, so the lesson is immediately clear: click tiles until the surrounding neighborhood matches the target kernel.nLater levels keep the exact same objective, but add strategy through click propagation. Some special clickable tiles no longer affect only themselves: when clicked, they flip a small local pattern such as a row, a column, a plus, or a full 3×3 burst centered on themselves. These special tiles must still be easy to recognize visually, but the puzzle should always remain about making one or more local neighborhoods match their target kernels. The added difficulty should come from overlapping effects, shared tiles, sequencing, and move optimization, not from introducing a new symbolic rule system.The visual style should stay bold and minimal. The live board tiles should be large square modules with strong negative space between them. The goal kernel should also be large and readable, not compressed into a tiny icon. The player should instantly understand that the center shows the reference color and the 8 surrounding preview cells describe the desired final arrangement of the 8 surrounding live tiles.Every click spends one unit of the move timer. If the timer reaches zero before all goal kernels are satisfied, the level is lost. Level 1 may include a small feedback flash for clicking outside a valid tile, just to teach that only the large square modules are interactable.The whole game has exactly 6 levels. Level 1 should teach almost the entire base game with a single obvious neighborhood and self-only toggles. Later levels can introduce multiple goal kernels, overlapping neighborhoods, shared tiles, and special propagation tiles, but the visual and logical identity of the game must remain the same: a clean local pattern-matching puzzle where you transform surrounding tiles to match a shown target kernel.
